summary: This chapter delves into incomes exempt from total income, focusing intensely on agricultural income, its exact definition, and the critical rules for apportioning composite business and agricultural income (Rules 270 & 271). It covers the precise mathematical mechanism of partial integration of agricultural income for individuals and HUFs. Additionally, it highlights other exempt incomes like partner share from firms, MP/MLA allowances, and the strict disallowance of expenditure related to exempt income under Section 14.

oneword.q: What percentage of income from the sale of tea grown and manufactured in India is treated as agricultural income?
What percentage of income from the sale of rubber products manufactured in India is treated as business income?
Is the income from breeding livestock or dairy farming considered agricultural income?
Under which section are expenses related to earning exempt income disallowed?
Does partial integration of agricultural income apply to a domestic company?

sa.q: Explain the rules for treating agricultural land as 'Urban' based on aerial distance.
sa.a: Agricultural land is urban if it is outside municipal limits but within: 2 km if population is >10,000 up to 1,00,000; 6 km if population is >1,00,000 up to 10,00,000; 8 km if population is >10,00,000.

sa.q: How is income apportioned when an assessee grows sugarcane and uses it to manufacture sugar in their own factory?
sa.a: Under Rule 270, the market value of the sugarcane used as raw material is allowed as a deduction to compute the business income from sugar manufacturing. That market value, minus the cost of cultivating the sugarcane, constitutes the exempt agricultural income.

sa.q: What are the two conditions necessary for applying the partial integration of agricultural income?
sa.a: 1) The net agricultural income must exceed ₹5,000 p.a., and 2) The non-agricultural income must exceed the basic exemption limit.

essay.q: Mr. Vikas grows sugarcane and uses it to manufacture sugar. 40% of his sugarcane is sold directly for ₹12 lakhs (cost of cultivation ₹6 lakhs). The remaining 60% is used for sugar manufacturing (cost of cultivation ₹15 lakhs, market value ₹25 lakhs). After incurring ₹1.5 lakhs in manufacturing, the sugar was sold for ₹30 lakhs. Compute his business and agricultural income.
essay.a:
1. Business Income from Sugar: Sale proceeds (₹30,00,000) - Market value of sugarcane used (₹25,00,000) - Manufacturing expenses (₹1,50,000) = ₹3,50,000.
2. Agricultural Income from Sugar: Market value of sugarcane used (₹25,00,000) - Cost of cultivation (₹15,00,000) = ₹10,00,000.
3. Agricultural Income from direct sale: Sale proceeds (₹12,00,000) - Cost of cultivation (₹6,00,000) = ₹6,00,000.
Total Business Income = ₹3,50,000. Total Agricultural Income = ₹16,00,000.

computation.title: Computation of Business Income and Agricultural Income of Mr. Vikas
notes: As per Rule 270 of the Income-tax Rules, where agricultural produce is used as raw material in an industrial process, the market value of such produce is deducted from manufacturing revenues to determine Business Income.
The excess of market value over the cost of cultivation constitutes Agricultural Income exempt from tax under Section 10(1).

essay.q: Mr. Nilesh manufactures rubber from latex obtained from plants grown by him in India. He sells the latex for ₹36 lakhs. The cost of growing the plants is ₹16 lakhs and manufacturing cost is ₹12 lakhs. Compute his total income.
essay.a:
Total profit = ₹36,00,000 (sales) - ₹16,00,000 (growing cost) - ₹12,00,000 (manufacturing) = ₹8,00,000.
According to Rule 271, for rubber products manufactured from plants grown in India, composite income is apportioned as 65% agricultural income and 35% business income.
Agricultural Income = 65% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹5,20,000.
Business Income = 35% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹2,80,000.

computation.title: Computation of Business Income and Agricultural Income of Mr. Nilesh
computation.subtitle: (As per Rule 271 of Income-tax Rules)

rows.text: Sale proceeds of rubber products manufactured from latex grown in India
Less: Cost of growing latex plants

notes: Under Rule 271 of the Income-tax Rules, 35% of the composite profit from the manufacture of rubber is taxable as Business Income, and the remaining 65% is exempt as Agricultural Income.

essay.q: Mr. X (aged 40) has a salary income of ₹11,50,000, house property income of ₹3,80,000, and net agricultural income of ₹2,90,000 (after deducting expenses). Compute his tax liability for T.Y. 2026-27 under the default tax regime.
essay.a:
1. Non-agricultural income = ₹11,50,000 + ₹3,80,000 = ₹15,30,000.
2. Since agricultural income (₹2,90,000) > ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income > ₹4,00,000, partial integration applies.
3. Step 1 (Xn): Tax on Aggregate Income (₹15,30,000 + ₹2,90,000 = ₹18,20,000) under default regime. Tax = ₹1,64,000.
4. Step 2 (Yn): Tax on (Agricultural Income ₹2,90,000 + Basic Exemption ₹4,00,000 = ₹6,90,000). Tax = ₹14,500.
5. Step 3: Tax Chargeable = Xn - Yn = ₹1,64,000 - ₹14,500 = ₹1,49,500.
6. Add Health and Education Cess @4% = ₹5,980.
7. Total Tax Liability = ₹1,55,480.

computation.title: Computation of Total Income and Tax Liability of Mr. X
computation.subtitle: (Assessment Year 2027-28 / Tax Year 2026-27 - Default Tax Regime)

rows.text: I. Computation of Non-Agricultural Total Income
Net Agricultural Income (for rate integration purpose only)
II. Computation of Tax Liability (Partial Integration Method)
Step 2: Tax on (Agri Income ₹2,90,000 + Basic Exemption ₹4,00,000 = ₹6,90,000)

notes: Partial integration applies because net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit (₹4,00,000 under the default tax regime).
Agricultural income is not taxed directly; it is integrated solely to determine the tax rate on non-agricultural income.
